# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.
- If you are updating or improving an artifact that already exists, re-use its same `id` so that your new version replaces the old one rather than creating a duplicate.

## Never allowed — always stripped, even if instructed
<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.
<a href> to external sites is fine. Inline data: image URIs are fine.

## Design
Single column, max-width ~760px, centred. No animations, gradients, shadows, emojis, or decorative icons. SVG only for data visualisation.
Font: `-apple-system, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif`, ~14–15px, line-height ~1.6.
Palette: bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f7f8fa`, border `#e5e7eb`, text `#1f2328`, muted `#57606a`, accent `#3b82d4` (sparingly), secondary `#7c5cd8` (rarely).

# office_read — structured Office file reading
Use `office_read` to read content from .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx files. For anything beyond basic text extraction — path syntax, property names, format-specific strategies — load the `office-insights` skill first using the `use_skill` tool.
Prefer `mode: text` for full extraction, `mode: outline` for structure, `mode: get` with a `query` path for a specific element, `mode: validate` for OpenXML schema validation, `mode: dump` to materialise the full document to disk for scripted analysis of large files.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# office_edit — structured Office file editing
Always load the `office-insights` skill (via `use_skill`) before editing — it contains path syntax, property names, and format-specific rules.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:**
The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Parallel `office_edit` calls in the same turn WILL corrupt the document or crash the resident.
**Use `operation:batch` when adding multiple elements (e.g. a full slide with shapes).** A batch is ONE tool call containing a JSON array of operations — it opens the document once, applies all operations, and saves once. This is faster and avoids the parallelism trap entirely.
Correct pattern for adding a slide with two shapes — ONE tool call:
  office_edit operation:batch ops:'[{"command":"add","parent":"/","type":"slide"},{"command":"add","parent":"/slide[last()]","type":"shape","props":{"text":"Title"}}]'
Only fall back to sequential single calls when operations depend on the result of the previous one (e.g. reading back a path before using it).

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

# grep — content search
Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.
Use `read_file` only after grep tells you which file and lines to look at.

For factual questions that require knowledge about IBM products, platforms, languages, commands, APIs, configuration, documented behavior, compatibility, or product-specific errors, consult IBM documentation before answering.
This includes technologies such as IBM i, IBM Z, z/OS, Db2, CICS, COBOL, JCL, RPG, AIX, and watsonx, even when the user does not explicitly say IBM.
For Bob(or IBM Bob) product questions, call `search_ibm_docs` directly with `library_name: "bob"`.
For other IBM products, first call `list_ibm_doc_libraries`, select the most relevant exact library name from its response, and then call `search_ibm_docs`. Do not invent or modify library names.
You may reuse a library name already returned in the current conversation for follow-up questions about the same product.
Base factual product claims on the retrieved documentation. If no suitable library or relevant documentation is found, say so rather than guessing.
Documentation lookup is unnecessary when the request is purely about code in the workspace and does not require IBM product knowledge.

# Subagents
You have access to `spawn_subagent` which creates an independent agent with its own context.

**Default: do the work yourself.** Most tasks are faster and cheaper without a subagent.
Only consider a subagent when ALL of these apply:
- The task is clearly self-contained and only needs a summary back
- It would add significant irrelevant content to your context
- You cannot accomplish it with 1-2 direct tool calls

Available types:
- "explore": Explore codebase (read tools, explorer model)
- "general": Inherits current mode tools, default model

**fork_context**: Set to true when the subagent needs to understand prior conversation — e.g., decisions made, constraints discovered, or user preferences expressed earlier.
Leave false (default) when the description alone is sufficient context.

Do NOT use subagents for:
- Simple file reads, searches, or single-tool operations
- Tasks where you already have relevant context
- Quick lookups that would take fewer turns done directly

# create_chart — chart output
Use the `create_chart` tool when the user asks for a chart or data visualisation.

## How it works
Call the tool with:
- `type`: one of LineChart | BarChart | PieChart | ScatterChart | RadarChart | BoxplotChart
- `title`: short human-readable title for the chart tile
- `props`: a JSON string of chart-specific props

The props JSON must be valid for the chosen chart type. Do NOT wrap it in a spec fence.
Example for BarChart:
{"xAxisData":["Jan","Feb","Mar"],"series":[{"name":"Revenue","data":[4200,5800,3900]}],"title":"Monthly Revenue"}

Activate the `create-chart` skill before building props to get the full per-type prop schemas.

2 | 
3 | This prompt file defines **three specialist subagent personas** and an
4 | orchestration contract. The Node.js orchestration script at

10 | ## AGENT 1 — RED TEAM (Adversarial Fuzzer)

12 | ```
13 | SYSTEM PROMPT — RED TEAM AGENT
14 | ================================
15 | You are an elite, adversarial Red Team security engineer. Your sole purpose
16 | is to break the target API. You have no interest in fixing anything — you
17 | exist to discover and prove vulnerabilities.
18 | 
19 | TARGET: POST /api/v1/transfer  (Express.js route in demo-app/routes/transfer.js)
20 | SPEC:   demo-app/openapi.json
21 | 
22 | YOUR MISSION:
23 |   1. Read the current source of `demo-app/routes/transfer.js`.
24 |   2. Read the OpenAPI spec at `demo-app/openapi.json`.
25 |   3. Analyse every input boundary, type assumption, concurrency window, and
26 |      business-logic constraint exposed by the route.
27 |   4. Generate or overwrite `demo-app/tests/generated_fuzzing.test.js` with an
28 |      exhaustive Jest/supertest attack suite that targets:
29 |        - Null / undefined / missing required fields
30 |        - Negative, zero, NaN, Infinity, and -Infinity amounts
31 |        - Non-numeric amounts: strings, arrays, objects, booleans
32 |        - Oversized payloads (amount > all possible balances combined)
33 |        - Type-confusion attacks: numeric senderId, object recipientId
34 |        - Prototype-pollution vectors: __proto__, constructor, toString keys
35 |        - NoSQL-injection objects: { "$gt": 0 }, { "$ne": null }
36 |        - SQL-injection strings in senderId / recipientId
37 |        - Unicode / emoji / null-byte strings in string fields
38 |        - Empty-string senderId or recipientId
39 |        - senderId === recipientId (self-transfer)
40 |        - Amount precision attacks: 0.0000000001, Number.EPSILON
41 |   5. Generate or overwrite `demo-app/tests/generated_concurrency.test.js`
42 |      with race-condition tests that fire 10–20 simultaneous identical requests
43 |      to drain the sender's entire balance, asserting that at most one succeeds
44 |      and the final balance is never negative.
45 |   6. Run `npm test` inside `demo-app/` using the terminal.
46 |   7. Capture the full terminal output (stdout + stderr).
47 |   8. Produce a structured ATTACK REPORT with the following JSON shape and
48 |      print it as the LAST thing you output so the orchestrator can parse it:
49 | 
50 |      {
51 |        "agent": "RED_TEAM",
52 |        "round": <integer, starting at 1>,
53 |        "totalTests": <number>,
54 |        "passing": <number>,
55 |        "failing": <number>,
56 |        "vulnerabilities": [
57 |          {
58 |            "id": "VULN-<n>",
59 |            "severity": "CRITICAL|HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW",
60 |            "description": "<one-sentence description>",
61 |            "payload": "<the exact payload or test case that exposed it>",
62 |            "httpStatus": <status code actually returned>,
63 |            "expectedStatus": <status code that should have been returned>
64 |          }
65 |        ],

67 |      }

69 | RULES:
70 |   - Be aggressive. If the route handles something gracefully, probe deeper.
71 |   - Never modify `routes/transfer.js`. You only write test files.
72 |   - If all tests pass and vulnerabilities is empty, set "passing" equal to
73 |     "totalTests" and still emit the JSON report so the Judge can evaluate.
74 |   - Do NOT add explanatory prose after the JSON block.
75 | ```

128 | ## AGENT 3 — JUDGE (Evaluator & Termination Authority)
129 | 
130 | ```
131 | SYSTEM PROMPT — JUDGE AGENT
132 | =============================
133 | You are an impartial security audit Judge. You hold the veto power that ends
134 | the Red Team / Blue Team loop. You accept no excuses and issue no leniency.
135 | 
136 | YOUR INPUTS (provided by the orchestrator in the user message):
137 |   - The Red Team ATTACK REPORT JSON from the current round.
138 |   - The Blue Team PATCH REPORT JSON from the current round.
139 |   - A history of all previous round summaries (may be empty on round 1).
140 | 
141 | YOUR MISSION:
142 |   1. Cross-reference every vulnerability in the ATTACK REPORT against the
143 |      PATCH REPORT. Verify that each VULN-n has a corresponding patch entry.
144 |   2. Assess patch quality:
145 |        - Does the strategy actually close the vector, or is it superficial?
146 |        - Could the patch introduce regressions in legitimate traffic?
147 |        - Are there classes of attack the Red Team did NOT test but the route
148 |          is still obviously vulnerable to?
149 |   3. Check progress across rounds: if the same vulnerability reappears across
150 |      two or more rounds, escalate its severity by one level and flag it.
151 |   4. Decide: APPROVED or REJECTED.
152 |        APPROVED  — all reported vulnerabilities are patched, no regressions
153 |                    introduced, and you have no residual concerns.
154 |        REJECTED  — one or more vulnerabilities remain unpatched, patches are
155 |                    insufficient, or new vulnerability classes are obvious.
156 |   5. Produce a JUDGE VERDICT with the following JSON shape and print it as
157 |      the LAST thing you output:
158 | 
159 |      {
160 |        "agent": "JUDGE",
161 |        "round": <same integer>,
162 |        "verdict": "APPROVED" | "REJECTED",
163 |        "score": <integer 0–100, security posture score after this round>,
164 |        "approvedVulns": [ "<VULN-n>", ... ],
165 |        "rejectedVulns": [
166 |          {
167 |            "vulnId": "<VULN-n>",
168 |            "reason": "<why the patch is insufficient or the vuln is still open>",
169 |            "suggestedStrategy": "<one-sentence hint for Blue Team next round>"
170 |          }
171 |        ],
172 |        "newConcerns": [
173 |          "<any attack class not yet tested that should be added next round>"
174 |        ],
175 |        "summary": "<2–3 sentence plain-English verdict summary>"
176 |      }
177 | 
178 | RULES:
179 |   - You are the only agent that can set "verdict": "APPROVED".
180 |   - If vulnerabilities is empty in the attack report AND all prior rounds are
181 |     clean, you MAY approve — but only after verifying the test suite is
182 |     genuinely comprehensive, not just shallow.
183 |   - Be skeptical. A route that passes 12 tests is not necessarily secure.
184 |   - Do NOT add explanatory prose after the JSON block.
185 | ```
186 | 
187 | ---
188 | 
189 | ## ORCHESTRATION CONTRACT
190 | 
191 | The script at `breakpoint-ai/scripts/orchestrate.js` drives the loop:
192 | 
193 | ```
194 | Round N
195 |   1. RED TEAM  reads the route + spec, runs npm test, emits ATTACK REPORT JSON.
196 |   2. BLUE TEAM receives ATTACK REPORT, patches the route, emits PATCH REPORT JSON.
197 |   3. JUDGE     receives both reports + history, emits JUDGE VERDICT JSON.
198 |   4. If verdict === "APPROVED"  → loop exits, final report written.
199 |      If verdict === "REJECTED"  → N++ and loop restarts from step 1.
200 |   5. Hard cap: 5 rounds. If not approved by round 5, the script exits with
201 |      code 1 and writes a FAILED audit report.
202 | ```

Now I have a complete picture of what this product is. Here's a direct, honest breakdown:

---

## What BreakPoint AI Actually Is

**It's an MCP server + orchestration tool** — not an app you install from a store, not a VS Code extension, not an executable. It's a Node.js background service that plugs into an AI coding assistant (Bob/Claude) via the **Model Context Protocol**.

---

## The Three Pieces

```
breakpoint-ai/
├── mcp-server/        ← The core product. A Node.js process that runs in the background.
├── scripts/           ← orchestrate.js: the Red/Blue/Judge AI loop runner
└── dashboard/         ← A local React+Express web UI (optional, runs on localhost)
```

### 1. [`mcp-server/src/index.ts`](breakpoint-ai/mcp-server/src/index.ts) — The actual product
This is a **stdio MCP server**. Bob (or any MCP-compatible AI client) talks to it over stdin/stdout. It exposes tools like `get_git_diff`, `run_fuzzer`, `read_test_logs`, `apply_patch`, and a static analysis scanner. When Bob calls `run_fuzzer`, it shells out and runs Jest tests on whatever codebase it's pointed at.

### 2. [`scripts/orchestrate.js`](breakpoint-ai/scripts/orchestrate.js) — The AI loop
This calls IBM watsonx.ai directly via REST. It reads your route file, sends it to Granite, gets attack/patch/judge reports back in JSON, loops up to 5 rounds. **This is completely standalone** — it doesn't need Bob at all, just `WATSONX_API_KEY` and `WATSONX_PROJECT_ID`.

### 3. [`dashboard/server.js`](breakpoint-ai/dashboard/server.js) — The UI
An Express server + React frontend. Shows audit reports, test results, live SSE log streaming. Runs on `localhost:3000` or wherever you point it.

---

## How a Dev Would Actually Use It

### The MCP server path (for use inside Bob/AI assistants)

```
# Install once, globally
cd breakpoint-ai/mcp-server
npm install && npm run build
npm install -g .          # puts 'breakpoint-mcp' on your PATH
```

Then in your Bob MCP config (`~/.bob/mcp_settings.json` or equivalent), register it **once** globally — it lives outside any project:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "breakpoint": {
      "command": "breakpoint-mcp",
      "args": [],
      "env": {
        "WATSONX_API_KEY": "your-key"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Bob starts it as a background process automatically on launch. It stays running as long as Bob is open. **You don't touch it again.** Any project you open in Bob gets access to the tools — because the config is global, not per-project.

---

### The standalone orchestrator path (CI/CD or no AI assistant needed)

For a dev who has a program anywhere on their drive and wants to audit it:

```powershell
# Point it at any project, anywhere
$env:WATSONX_API_KEY   = "your-key"
$env:WATSONX_PROJECT_ID = "your-project-id"
$env:DEMO_APP_PATH     = "C:\Users\You\any-project-folder"

node C:\path\to\breakpoint-ai\scripts\orchestrate.js
```

The `DEMO_APP_PATH` env var overrides the hardcoded path — so it works on **any project kept anywhere on your drive**, not just in the breakpoint-ai folder.

---

### The dashboard path (just want a UI)

```powershell
cd breakpoint-ai/dashboard
npm install
npm start      # opens localhost:3000
```

---

## What Needs to Change to Make This "Real Product" Grade

Right now it has two friction points that block real adoption:

| Problem | What it is | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `DEMO_APP_PATH` is hardcoded fallback to `demo-app/` | The orchestrator defaults to its own demo | Make `--target` a required CLI arg, not optional |
| MCP server's `DEMO_APP_DIR` is hardcoded relative to `__dirname` | [`index.ts:48`](breakpoint-ai/mcp-server/src/index.ts:48) `path.resolve(__dirname, "..", "..", "demo-app")` | Read it from an env var `BREAKPOINT_TARGET` instead, so the MCP server can be installed globally but aimed at any project |

Those two changes are what separate "prototype that only works in its own folder" from "tool a dev can run against any project on their machine without copying files around."

---

## Summary: What it is

| | Answer |
|---|---|
| **What is it?** | An MCP server (Node.js stdio process) + a standalone Node.js CLI script |
| **Where does it live?** | Installed once globally via `npm install -g`, or kept in one folder and called via absolute path |
| **Do devs reinstall per project?** | No — one global install, pointed at any project via env var |
| **Does it need Bob?** | No — `orchestrate.js` talks to watsonx directly; Bob just gives it a nicer interface |
| **Is it a web app?** | The dashboard is, but it's local (`localhost`), not hosted |
| **Is it an extension?** | No — it's an MCP server, which means it works with any MCP-compatible AI client (Bob, Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.) |

Here's exactly what was built and how it all fits together now:

---

## What was built

A new `breakpoint-ai/cli/` package — a fully standalone Node.js CLI tool. **Zero dependency on Bob, MCP, VS Code, or any specific folder layout.**

### Files created

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`cli/bin/breakpoint.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/bin/breakpoint.js) | Entry point that goes on your PATH. Routes to sub-commands. |
| [`cli/lib/audit.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/lib/audit.js) | The full Red→Blue→Judge loop. Talks directly to watsonx. |
| [`cli/lib/scan.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/lib/scan.js) | Static analysis. No AI, no network. Works on anything. |
| [`cli/lib/scan-lib.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/lib/scan-lib.js) | 14 security rules shared between scan and audit. |
| [`cli/lib/discover.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/lib/discover.js) | Probes any project for its test runner, source files, API spec. |
| [`cli/lib/run-tests-lib.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/lib/run-tests-lib.js) | Runs jest, vitest, mocha, or pytest — auto-detected. |
| [`cli/lib/run-tests.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/lib/run-tests.js) | `breakpoint run-tests` command. |
| [`cli/lib/init.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/lib/init.js) | `breakpoint init` — writes `breakpoint.config.json` to any project. |
| [`cli/lib/dash.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/lib/dash.js) | Dashboard server rewritten to work on any target dir. |

### Files patched

- [`mcp-server/src/index.ts`](breakpoint-ai/mcp-server/src/index.ts) — `DEMO_APP_DIR` and `WORKSPACE_ROOT` now read from `BREAKPOINT_TARGET` env var at startup instead of being hardcoded to `../../demo-app`.
- [`dashboard/server.js`](breakpoint-ai/dashboard/server.js) — same `BREAKPOINT_TARGET` resolution.

---

## How a dev uses it on their own project, anywhere on their drive

**Install once, globally:**
```powershell
npm install -g D:\Aryav\Hackathons\IBM Bob 2.0\breakpoint-ai\cli
# or after publishing: npm install -g breakpoint-ai
```

**Then from any project, any path:**
```powershell
# One-time setup (writes a config to the project)
breakpoint init --target C:\Users\you\my-app

# Static scan — no AI, instant, works offline
breakpoint scan --target C:\Users\you\my-app --severity high

# Full AI audit
$env:WATSONX_API_KEY   = "your-key"
$env:WATSONX_PROJECT_ID = "your-project"
breakpoint audit --target C:\Users\you\my-app

# Dashboard in the browser
breakpoint dash --target C:\Users\you\my-app

# Just run the tests
breakpoint run-tests --target C:\Users\you\my-app
```

**Or set a permanent default so you don't type `--target` every time:**
```powershell
$env:BREAKPOINT_TARGET = "C:\Users\you\my-app"
breakpoint audit   # uses the env var automatically
```

The tool auto-detects the test runner (Jest, Vitest, Mocha, pytest), finds the OpenAPI spec if one exists, and respects a `breakpoint.config.json` in the project root if you want to customize anything.

data.content: Let me read the actual watsonx integration code to give you a grounded answer.

That's everything I need to know. Here's the straight answer:

---

## The AI it uses: IBM watsonx.ai (cloud API)

The tool calls **IBM watsonx.ai** over HTTPS. Specifically:

- **Auth endpoint:** `https://iam.cloud.ibm.com/identity/token` — IBM's IAM service exchanges your API key for a bearer token
- **Inference endpoint:** `https://us-south.ml.cloud.ibm.com/ml/v1/text/chat` — the watsonx model API
- **Default model:** `ibm/granite-3-3-8b-instruct` (IBM Granite)

This is a **cloud API call**, not a local model. The tool sends your source code to IBM's servers, gets back the Red Team attack report / Blue Team patch / Judge verdict as JSON, and applies it.

---

## What you need on any computer

### Hard requirements — nothing works without these

| Requirement | What it is | Where to get it |
|---|---|---|
| **Node.js 18+** | Runs the CLI itself | [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org) |
| **`WATSONX_API_KEY`** | IBM Cloud API key | IBM Cloud console → Manage → Access → API keys |
| **`WATSONX_PROJECT_ID`** | Your watsonx.ai project ID | watsonx.ai → Projects → your project → Manage tab |

That's it. No IDE. No VS Code. No Bob. No Docker. No Python. Nothing else.

### Soft requirements — only needed for specific commands

| Requirement | When needed |
|---|---|
| **npm** (comes with Node.js) | If the target project uses Jest/Vitest/Mocha |
| **Python 3 + pytest** | Only if the target project uses pytest |
| **git** | Only for the `get_git_diff` tool in the MCP server |

---

## Complete setup on a brand new machine

```powershell
# 1. Install Node.js 18+ from nodejs.org — that's the only software install

# 2. Install breakpoint globally (one time, stays forever)
npm install -g breakpoint-ai
# or from local folder:
npm install -g "D:\path\to\breakpoint-ai\cli"

# 3. Set your credentials — do this once per machine (or put in your shell profile)
$env:WATSONX_API_KEY    = "your-ibm-cloud-api-key"
$env:WATSONX_PROJECT_ID = "your-watsonx-project-id"

# 4. Point it at any project and go
breakpoint scan  --target C:\any\project\anywhere
breakpoint audit --target C:\any\project\anywhere
breakpoint dash  --target C:\any\project\anywhere
```

To make the credentials permanent so you never type them again, add them to your PowerShell profile:

```powershell
# Open your profile file
notepad $PROFILE

# Add these two lines to it:
$env:WATSONX_API_KEY    = "your-key"
$env:WATSONX_PROJECT_ID = "your-project-id"
```

---

## What happens to your code

Your source files are sent to IBM watsonx.ai's API to generate the attack reports and patches. IBM's data handling policies apply. The `scan` command — static analysis — **never sends anything anywhere**, so if you're on an air-gapped machine or don't have credentials yet, `breakpoint scan` still works fully offline.

---

## The `scan` command needs zero AI

```powershell
# Works completely offline, no keys, no account needed
breakpoint scan --target C:\any\project --severity high --format json
```

This runs 14 built-in security rules (SQL injection, prototype pollution, hardcoded secrets, path traversal, etc.) directly against the source files locally. No network call. Instant results.

## WeatherGPT scan results — 3 files, 2 real issues

### 🟠 HIGH — [`app.py` line 575](D:\Aryav\Hackathons\SIH 2026\Internal Hackathon\WeatherGPT\app.py) — Flask debug mode on
```python
app.run(debug=True, port=5000)
```
**Why it matters:** `debug=True` activates Werkzeug's interactive debugger. If someone hits an error page on a deployed server, they get an in-browser Python REPL with full access to your server. It's literally remote code execution. Change to:
```python
app.run(debug=False, port=5000)
# or better — read from env:
app.run(debug=os.environ.get('FLASK_DEBUG', 'false').lower() == 'true', port=5000)
```

### 🟡 MEDIUM — [`app.py` line 571](D:\Aryav\Hackathons\SIH 2026\Internal Hackathon\WeatherGPT\app.py) — `render_template_string`
```python
return render_template_string(HTML_PAGE)
```
**Why it matters:** `render_template_string` processes Jinja2 template syntax at runtime. If `HTML_PAGE` ever contains any user-supplied content, an attacker can inject `{{ 7*7 }}` or worse and get code execution (Server-Side Template Injection). If `HTML_PAGE` is entirely your own static string, this is low risk — but using `render_template('page.html')` with a file is safer practice.

### ⚪ INFO — `print()` in 5 places
Not a security issue, just a production hygiene note. `print()` goes to stdout with no timestamps or log levels — harder to monitor in deployment. `import logging` handles this properly.

  '.lock',   // package-lock.json is text but has no security value
]);

const MAX_FILE_BYTES = 500 * 1024; // 500 KB

// Lines longer than this indicate a minified file — skip the whole file
const MAX_LINE_LENGTH = 2000;

/**
 * Returns true if a file should be skipped for scanning.
 */
function shouldSkipFile(filePath, stat) {
  const ext = path.extname(filePath).toLowerCase();
  if (BINARY_EXTENSIONS.has(ext)) return true;
  if (stat && stat.size > MAX_FILE_BYTES) return true;
  return false;
}

/**
 * Returns true if the file content looks minified (any line > MAX_LINE_LENGTH).
 */
function isMinified(src) {
  const newline = src.indexOf('\n');
  // If the first line is very long, treat as minified
  const firstLine = newline === -1 ? src : src.slice(0, newline);
  return firstLine.length > MAX_LINE_LENGTH;
}

 * Runs all rules against src line-by-line.
 * Skips rules whose `exts` array doesn't include the file's extension.
 * Returns an array of finding objects.
 */
function runAstRules(filePath, src) {
  if (isMinified(src)) return []; // skip minified files silently

  const ext      = path.extname(filePath).toLowerCase();
  const lines    = src.split('\n');
  const findings = [];
  for (const rule of AST_RULES) {
    // If the rule declares an extension filter, skip it for other file types
    if (rule.exts && !rule.exts.includes(ext)) continue;
    for (let i = 0; i < lines.length; i++) {
      if (rule.pattern.test(lines[i])) {
        findings.push({
          file:     filePath,
          rule:     rule.id,
          severity: rule.severity,
          line:     i + 1,
          snippet:  lines[i].trim().slice(0, 200),
          hint:     rule.hint,
        });
      }
    }
  }
  return findings;
}

 * `excludeDirs` is an optional array of directory names to skip
 * (in addition to the built-in defaults).
 * Skips binary files and files over MAX_FILE_BYTES.

const DEFAULT_SKIP = new Set([
  'node_modules', 'build', '.git', 'dist', 'coverage',
  '.breakpoint', '__pycache__', '.venv', '.venv-clean',
  '.idea', '.mypy_cache', '.pytest_cache', '.tox', 'venv', 'env',
  'vendor',   // Go, PHP, Ruby
  'target',   // Rust, Java/Maven
  'bin', 'obj', // .NET
  '.gradle', '.mvn', // Java build tools
  'Pods',     // iOS
]);

function collectSourceFiles(dir, extensions, excludeDirs) {
  const results  = [];
  const skipDirs = new Set([...DEFAULT_SKIP, ...(excludeDirs || [])]);

  // Normalise extensions to lowercase for case-insensitive matching
  const normExts = extensions
    ? extensions.map(e => e.toLowerCase())
    : null;

  function walk(current) {
    let entries;
    try { entries = fs.readdirSync(current); } catch { return; }
    for (const entry of entries) {
      if (skipDirs.has(entry)) continue;
      const full = path.join(current, entry);
      let stat;
      try { stat = fs.statSync(full); } catch { continue; }
      if (stat.isDirectory()) {
        walk(full);
      } else {
        const ext = path.extname(entry).toLowerCase();
        if (normExts && !normExts.includes(ext)) continue;
        if (shouldSkipFile(full, stat)) continue;
        results.push(full);
      }
    }
  }

  walk(dir);
  return results;
}

/**
 * Returns the set of all file extensions the scanner has rules for.
 * Useful for auto-populating breakpoint.config.json extensions.
 */
function getSupportedExtensions() {
  const exts = new Set();
  for (const rule of AST_RULES) {
    if (rule.exts) rule.exts.forEach(e => exts.add(e));
  }
  return [...exts].sort();
}

/**
 * Runs all rules against src line-by-line.
 * Skips rules whose `exts` array doesn't include the file's extension.
 * Returns an array of finding objects.
 */
function runAstRules(filePath, src) {
  const ext      = path.extname(filePath).toLowerCase();
  const lines    = src.split('\n');
  const findings = [];
  for (const rule of AST_RULES) {
    // If the rule declares an extension filter, skip it for other file types
    if (rule.exts && !rule.exts.includes(ext)) continue;
    for (let i = 0; i < lines.length; i++) {
      if (rule.pattern.test(lines[i])) {
        findings.push({
          file:     filePath,
          rule:     rule.id,
          severity: rule.severity,
          line:     i + 1,
          snippet:  lines[i].trim().slice(0, 200),
          hint:     rule.hint,
        });
      }
    }
  }
  return findings;
}

/**
 * Recursively collects files matching `extensions` under `dir`.
 * `excludeDirs` is an optional array of directory names to skip
 * (in addition to the built-in defaults).
 */
const DEFAULT_SKIP = new Set(['node_modules', 'build', '.git', 'dist', 'coverage',
                               '.breakpoint', '__pycache__', '.venv', '.venv-clean',
                               '.idea', '.mypy_cache', '.pytest_cache', '.tox', 'venv', 'env']);

function collectSourceFiles(dir, extensions, excludeDirs) {
  const results  = [];
  const skipDirs = new Set([...DEFAULT_SKIP, ...(excludeDirs || [])]);

  function walk(current) {
    let entries;
    try { entries = fs.readdirSync(current); } catch { return; }
    for (const entry of entries) {
      if (skipDirs.has(entry)) continue;
      const full = path.join(current, entry);
      let stat;
      try { stat = fs.statSync(full); } catch { continue; }
      if (stat.isDirectory()) {
        walk(full);
      } else if (!extensions || extensions.includes(path.extname(entry).toLowerCase())) {
        results.push(full);
      }
    }
  }

  walk(dir);
  return results;
}

module.exports = { runAstRules, collectSourceFiles, AST_RULES };

// ── Helpers ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

// How many characters of source to include per LLM call.
// Granite-3-3-8b has ~8192 token context; ~3 chars/token → ~24K chars safe budget.
// We reserve ~8K for the system prompt + JSON output, leaving ~16K for source.
const SOURCE_BUDGET_CHARS = 16_000;

// How many chars to include per individual file (prevents one huge file consuming all budget)

// How many lines of context to extract around each finding for the Blue Team
const LINES_OF_CONTEXT = 20;

/**
 * Builds a source context string that fits within SOURCE_BUDGET_CHARS.
 *
 * Strategy for large projects:
 *   1. Skip test files, minified files, lock files.
 *   2. Prefer files that already have static findings (they're most relevant).
 *   3. Truncate each file to MAX_CHARS_PER_FILE to prevent one file consuming all budget.
 *   4. Stop adding files once the budget is hit.
 *   5. Include a file index at the top so the model knows what exists even if not shown.
 */
function buildSourceContext(targetDir, sourceFiles, staticFindings) {
  // Deduplicate file list into relevant (non-test) source files
  const isTestFile = f =>
    /[/\\]tests?[/\\]/.test(f) ||
    f.endsWith('.test.js')  || f.endsWith('.test.ts') ||
    f.endsWith('.spec.js')  || f.endsWith('.spec.ts') ||
    f.endsWith('_test.go')  || f.endsWith('_test.py');

  const relevant = sourceFiles.filter(f => !isTestFile(f));

  // Score files: ones with findings first, then by size ascending
  const findingFiles = new Set(
    (staticFindings && staticFindings.findings || []).map(f => f.file)
      .map(f => path.resolve(targetDir, f))
  );

  const scored = relevant.map(f => ({
    path:    f,
    score:   findingFiles.has(f) ? 0 : 1,   // 0 = has findings (higher priority)
    size:    (() => { try { return fs.statSync(f).size; } catch { return 0; } })(),
  }))
  .sort((a, b) => a.score - b.score || a.size - b.size);

  // Build an index header (always include, doesn't count toward file budget)
  const allRels  = relevant.map(f => path.relative(targetDir, f).replace(/\\/g, '/'));
  const indexHdr = `=== PROJECT FILE INDEX (${relevant.length} source files) ===\n` +
                   allRels.join('\n') + '\n';

  // Fill budget
  const sections = [indexHdr];
  let used = indexHdr.length;

  for (const { path: f } of scored) {
    if (used >= SOURCE_BUDGET_CHARS) break;
    const rel     = path.relative(targetDir, f).replace(/\\/g, '/');
    const raw     = readFileSafe(f);
    const content = raw.length > MAX_CHARS_PER_FILE

      : raw;

    sections.push(block);

    sections.push(`\n[${skipped} additional files omitted to fit context window — full list in FILE INDEX above]`);

data.content:
Here's exactly what was changed and why each piece matters for "any size, any language, any complexity":

---

## What was fixed

### Language coverage — [`scan-lib.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/lib/scan-lib.js)

Added **54 new security rules** across 6 languages:

| Language | Rules added | Key threats covered |
|---|---|---|
| **Java** | 7 | SQL injection via `PreparedStatement`, XXE, unsafe deserialisation, `Runtime.exec` |
| **Go** | 5 | `db.Query` with `fmt.Sprintf`, `exec.Command` with user input, path traversal |
| **PHP** | 7 | `$_GET`/`$_POST` in queries, `eval()`, remote file inclusion, `echo $_GET` XSS |
| **Ruby** | 6 | ActiveRecord string interpolation, backtick injection, mass assignment |
| **C#** | 5 | `SqlCommand` concatenation, XXE via `XmlDocument`, `Response.Redirect` |
| **Rust** | 4 | `Command::new` with user input, `unsafe {}` blocks, hardcoded secrets |

Each rule has an `exts` filter so Python rules never fire on JS files and vice versa.

### Binary/minified file guard — [`scan-lib.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/lib/scan-lib.js)

- **31 binary extensions** skipped before reading (`.pyc`, `.class`, `.jar`, `.wasm`, images, archives, etc.)
- **500 KB size cap** — files over this are skipped (generated code, vendored libraries)
- **Minification detection** — first line > 2000 chars means the file is bundled/minified, skip it
- **`vendor/`, `target/`, `Pods/`, `.gradle/`** added to default skip dirs for Go/Java/Ruby/iOS/Rust projects

### Context window management — [`audit.js`](breakpoint-ai/cli/lib/audit.js)

**Before:** dumped every source file in full as one giant string. A project with 50 files would produce a message 10× larger than the model's context window → truncated garbage JSON back.

**After — `buildSourceContext`:**
- Always includes a **file index** (filenames only) so the model knows the whole project structure
- Files with static findings are **prioritised first** — the model sees the most relevant code
- Each file is **capped at 6,000 chars** — one huge file can't starve everything else
- Total message is **capped at 16,000 chars** — fits inside Granite's context window reliably
- A footer tells the model how many files were omitted and references the index

**After — `getAffectedFiles` (Blue Team):**
- Instead of sending the full file for patching, sends only **±20 lines around each vulnerable line** with line numbers
- For a 1,000-line `app.py` with one vuln at line 575, Blue Team now receives ~40 lines instead of 24,000 chars
- Falls back to full file if it fits within budget

| **Java** | `.java` | SQL injection (PreparedStatement), XXE, unsafe deserialization (ObjectInputStream), Runtime.exec, path traversal (File constructor), hardcoded secrets |
| **Go** | `.go` | db.Query with fmt.Sprintf, exec.Command with user input, os.Open traversal, hardcoded secrets |
| **PHP** | `.php` | $_GET/$_POST in queries, system/shell_exec injection, eval(), remote file inclusion, echo XSS, hardcoded secrets |
| **Ruby** | `.rb` | ActiveRecord string interpolation, backtick injection, eval/instance_eval, mass assignment, hardcoded secrets |
| **C#** | `.cs` | SqlCommand concatenation, XmlDocument XXE, Response.Redirect open redirect, hardcoded secrets |
| **Rust** | `.rs` | Command::new with user input, unsafe blocks, hardcoded secrets |
| **C / C++** | `.c` `.h` `.cpp` `.cc` `.cxx` `.hpp` | gets/strcpy/sprintf buffer overflow, format string, system()/popen() injection, atoi overflow, use-after-free, C++ new without nothrow |
| **Kotlin** | `.kt` `.kts` | rawQuery SQL injection, hardcoded secrets, sensitive Android Log, implicit Intents |
| **Swift** | `.swift` | SQL injection, hardcoded secrets, force unwrap (!), plain HTTP, sensitive print() |
| **HTML** | `.html` `.htm` `.xhtml` | Inline `<script>`, inline event handlers (onclick etc.), plain HTTP URLs, password autocomplete |
| **CSS / SCSS / Sass / Less** | `.css` `.scss` `.sass` `.less` | CSS expression() XSS, external @import |
| **Shell** | `.sh` `.bash` `.zsh` `.fish` | eval/exec injection, curl-pipe-to-shell, hardcoded secrets, chmod 777 |
| **Dart / Flutter** | `.dart` | Hardcoded secrets, plain HTTP URIs, sensitive print() |
| **Scala** | `.scala` | SQL injection (string interpolation), hardcoded secrets |

Every rule is **extension-filtered** — a PHP rule never fires on a `.py` file, a C buffer overflow rule never fires on `.swift`. Every new extension is also guarded against binary files and the 500 KB size limit.

## How the dashboard works — for any computer

### What it is

It's a **local web server** that runs on your machine and opens in any browser. It has nothing to do with any cloud service — the server runs on `localhost`, your browser connects to it, and it streams live data via SSE (Server-Sent Events) as audits run. Nobody outside your machine can see it unless you deliberately expose it.

### Starting it — one command

```powershell
breakpoint dash --target C:\path\to\your\project --port 4242
```

Then open `http://localhost:4242` in any browser. That's it.

### What you see

| Panel | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Radar chart** | 6-axis security score (input validation, race conditions, auth bypass, payload fuzzing, error handling, patch coverage) — updates live as tests run |
| **Live log** | Every test line streamed in real time — pass/fail/warning/payload events colour-coded |
| **Timeline** | Chronological list of what happened during the audit |
| **Attack surface** | Which areas are clean vs vulnerable |

### Separate computer — what you need

The server runs **on the same machine as the code being audited**. You don't install anything on the separate computer — you just open a browser and point it at the IP:

```
# On the machine running the audit (server machine):
breakpoint dash --target C:\your\project --port 4242

# On any other computer on the same network:
# Open browser → http://192.168.1.xx:4242   (use the server machine's local IP)
```

To find the server machine's IP on Windows:
```powershell
(Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 | Where-Object {$_.IPAddress -notlike "127.*"}).IPAddress
```

### The UI is bundled — no separate install step

The React frontend is pre-built and ships inside the `cli/public/` folder of the package. When you do `npm install -g breakpoint-ai`, the compiled UI comes with it. You don't need Node, npm, or anything else on the machine where you open the browser — just a browser.

### The `--port` flag

Default is `4242`. If that port is taken, pick any free one:

```powershell
breakpoint dash --target C:\project --port 3000
breakpoint dash --target C:\project --port 8080
```

### Running it alongside an audit

You can run the dashboard in one terminal and the audit in another — they work independently. The dashboard listens for file changes and picks up audit reports as they're written:

```powershell
# Terminal 1 — keep dashboard open
breakpoint dash --target C:\project

# Terminal 2 — run audit (dashboard updates automatically)
breakpoint audit --target C:\project
```

# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.
- If you are updating or improving an artifact that already exists, re-use its same `id` so that your new version replaces the old one rather than creating a duplicate.

## Never allowed — always stripped, even if instructed
<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.
<a href> to external sites is fine. Inline data: image URIs are fine.

## Design
Single column, max-width ~760px, centred. No animations, gradients, shadows, emojis, or decorative icons. SVG only for data visualisation.
Font: `-apple-system, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif`, ~14–15px, line-height ~1.6.
Palette: bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f7f8fa`, border `#e5e7eb`, text `#1f2328`, muted `#57606a`, accent `#3b82d4` (sparingly), secondary `#7c5cd8` (rarely).

# Mode Switching

You can switch between different modes using the switch_mode tool. Each mode provides access to different capabilities and tools optimized for specific types of tasks.

**When to switch modes:**
- The user explicitly requests a mode switch
- You need a tool that is ONLY available in another mode and is absolutely required to complete the task

**DO NOT switch modes when:**
- You can accomplish the task with your current tools
- The request is ambiguous

Stay in your current mode unless there is an explicit, compelling reason to switch. When in doubt, do not switch.

# office_read — structured Office file reading
Use `office_read` to read content from .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx files. For anything beyond basic text extraction — path syntax, property names, format-specific strategies — load the `office-insights` skill first using the `use_skill` tool.
Prefer `mode: text` for full extraction, `mode: outline` for structure, `mode: get` with a `query` path for a specific element, `mode: validate` for OpenXML schema validation, `mode: dump` to materialise the full document to disk for scripted analysis of large files.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# office_edit — structured Office file editing
Always load the `office-insights` skill (via `use_skill`) before editing — it contains path syntax, property names, and format-specific rules.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:**
The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Parallel `office_edit` calls in the same turn WILL corrupt the document or crash the resident.
**Use `operation:batch` when adding multiple elements (e.g. a full slide with shapes).** A batch is ONE tool call containing a JSON array of operations — it opens the document once, applies all operations, and saves once. This is faster and avoids the parallelism trap entirely.
Correct pattern for adding a slide with two shapes — ONE tool call:
  office_edit operation:batch ops:'[{"command":"add","parent":"/","type":"slide"},{"command":"add","parent":"/slide[last()]","type":"shape","props":{"text":"Title"}}]'
Only fall back to sequential single calls when operations depend on the result of the previous one (e.g. reading back a path before using it).

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

# grep — content search
Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.
Use `read_file` only after grep tells you which file and lines to look at.

For factual questions that require knowledge about IBM products, platforms, languages, commands, APIs, configuration, documented behavior, compatibility, or product-specific errors, consult IBM documentation before answering.
This includes technologies such as IBM i, IBM Z, z/OS, Db2, CICS, COBOL, JCL, RPG, AIX, and watsonx, even when the user does not explicitly say IBM.
For Bob(or IBM Bob) product questions, call `search_ibm_docs` directly with `library_name: "bob"`.
For other IBM products, first call `list_ibm_doc_libraries`, select the most relevant exact library name from its response, and then call `search_ibm_docs`. Do not invent or modify library names.
You may reuse a library name already returned in the current conversation for follow-up questions about the same product.
Base factual product claims on the retrieved documentation. If no suitable library or relevant documentation is found, say so rather than guessing.
Documentation lookup is unnecessary when the request is purely about code in the workspace and does not require IBM product knowledge.

# Subagents
You have access to `spawn_subagent` which creates an independent agent with its own context.

**Default: do the work yourself.** Most tasks are faster and cheaper without a subagent.
Only consider a subagent when ALL of these apply:
- The task is clearly self-contained and only needs a summary back
- It would add significant irrelevant content to your context
- You cannot accomplish it with 1-2 direct tool calls

Available types:
- "explore": Explore codebase (read tools, explorer model)
- "general": Inherits current mode tools, default model

**fork_context**: Set to true when the subagent needs to understand prior conversation — e.g., decisions made, constraints discovered, or user preferences expressed earlier.
Leave false (default) when the description alone is sufficient context.

Do NOT use subagents for:
- Simple file reads, searches, or single-tool operations
- Tasks where you already have relevant context
- Quick lookups that would take fewer turns done directly

# create_chart — chart output
Use the `create_chart` tool when the user asks for a chart or data visualisation.

## How it works
Call the tool with:
- `type`: one of LineChart | BarChart | PieChart | ScatterChart | RadarChart | BoxplotChart
- `title`: short human-readable title for the chart tile
- `props`: a JSON string of chart-specific props

The props JSON must be valid for the chosen chart type. Do NOT wrap it in a spec fence.
Example for BarChart:
{"xAxisData":["Jan","Feb","Mar"],"series":[{"name":"Revenue","data":[4200,5800,3900]}],"title":"Monthly Revenue"}

Activate the `create-chart` skill before building props to get the full per-type prop schemas.

189 | ## ORCHESTRATION CONTRACT
190 | 
191 | The script at `breakpoint-ai/scripts/orchestrate.js` drives the loop:
192 | 
193 | ```
194 | Round N
195 |   1. RED TEAM  reads the route + spec, runs npm test, emits ATTACK REPORT JSON.
196 |   2. BLUE TEAM receives ATTACK REPORT, patches the route, emits PATCH REPORT JSON.
197 |   3. JUDGE     receives both reports + history, emits JUDGE VERDICT JSON.
198 |   4. If verdict === "APPROVED"  → loop exits, final report written.
199 |      If verdict === "REJECTED"  → N++ and loop restarts from step 1.
200 |   5. Hard cap: 5 rounds. If not approved by round 5, the script exits with
201 |      code 1 and writes a FAILED audit report.
202 | ```

3 | # BreakPoint AI — Merge Security Gate
4 | #
5 | # Triggers on every pull-request targeting the default branch.
6 | # Spins up the demo-app inside Docker, runs the full Jest fuzzing +
7 | # concurrency suite via ci-fuzzer.js, and posts a "Merge Confidence

9 | # causing the required status check to fail and blocking the merge.
10 | #
11 | # ── Required repository secrets ─────────────────────────────────────────────
12 | #   (none — GITHUB_TOKEN is automatically provided by Actions)

14 | # ── Required repository / environment variables (optional overrides) ─────────

82 |           path: /tmp/demo-app-image.tar.gz
83 |           retention-days: 1

91 |     needs: build-image
92 | 
93 |     steps:
94 |       - name: Checkout PR branch
95 |         uses: actions/checkout@v4
96 |         with:
97 |           fetch-depth: 0
98 |

101 |         uses: actions/setup-node@v4
102 |         with:
103 |           node-version: "20"
104 | 
105 |       # ── Download and load the pre-built Docker image ───────────────────────
106 |       - name: Download image artifact
107 |         uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
108 |         with:
109 |           name: demo-app-image
110 |           path: /tmp
111 | 
112 |       - name: Load Docker image

114 | 
115 |       # ── Start the demo-app container in the background ─────────────────────

117 |         id: container

120 |             --detach \
121 |             --rm \
122 |             --name breakpoint-demo-app \

arguments.title: BreakPoint AI — Developer Reference
arguments.description: Complete developer guide: architecture, file map, languages, run commands, agent roles, and future prospects for BreakPoint AI.
arguments.html:
BreakPoint AI

Developer Reference — Architecture, File Map, Run Commands, Agent Roles & Future Prospects

What Is This Project?

BreakPoint AI is an autonomous security testing platform built around a Red Team → Blue Team → Judge agentic loop. It targets a deliberately vulnerable Express.js microservice (POST /api/v1/transfer), hammers it with AI-generated fuzzing and race-condition attacks, patches the vulnerabilities it finds, and gates every pull request through an automated CI merge-confidence scorecard — all powered by IBM watsonx.ai (Granite) as the LLM backbone.

The project also ships an MCP server that plugs the entire fuzzer pipeline directly into IBM Bob (and any other MCP-compatible AI client), plus a live React + SSE dashboard for real-time visibility.

Languages & Technologies Used

LayerLanguage / TechPurpose
Target app + scriptsJavaScript (Node.js)Express server, routes, orchestrator, CI fuzzer
MCP serverTypeScriptMCP tool implementations compiled to JS
Dashboard front-endReact JSXVite + React 18 + Recharts + Tailwind CSS SPA
Dashboard back-endJavaScript (Node.js)Express API + SSE broadcast server
CI pipelineYAML (GitHub Actions)Automated Docker-based security gate on PRs
API contractJSON (OpenAPI 3.0)Schema for the transfer endpoint
ContainerisationDockerfileReproducible demo-app image for CI
Bob promptMarkdownSystem prompts injected into sub-agent personas

Complete File Map

demo-app/ — The Intentionally Vulnerable Target

FileWhat it Does
server.jsExpress app entry point. Mounts the transfer router at /api/v1. Exports app for supertest. Starts on port 3000.
routes/transfer.jsTHE target file. Implements POST /api/v1/transfer: in-memory accounts, per-sender mutex lock to prevent race conditions, amount/type validation guards (applied by Blue Team across rounds).
openapi.jsonOpenAPI 3.0 schema for the transfer endpoint. Red Team reads this to understand the intended contract.
tests/generated_fuzzing.test.jsAI-generated Jest+supertest attack suite. Covers null fields, negative/NaN/Infinity amounts, type confusion, prototype pollution, NoSQL/SQL injection, unicode, self-transfer, precision exploits.
tests/generated_concurrency.test.jsRace-condition tests: fires 10–20 simultaneous requests to drain the sender's balance and asserts the final balance never goes negative.
package.jsonDeclares npm start and npm test (Jest). Dependencies: express, jest, supertest.
DockerfileBuilds the demo-app container for CI. Used by the GitHub Actions workflow.

scripts/ — Automation

FileWhat it Does
orchestrate.jsThe main agentic loop. Calls IBM watsonx.ai (Granite model) with Red Team / Blue Team / Judge system prompts, applies patches, saves round reports to audit-reports/, iterates up to 5 rounds until the Judge approves. Needs WATSONX_API_KEY, WATSONX_PROJECT_ID.
ci-fuzzer.jsLightweight CI gate script. Runs Jest, parses output, builds a Markdown Merge Confidence Scorecard, posts it as a GitHub PR comment, and exits with code 1 to block the merge on failure.

mcp-server/ — Bob Integration

FileWhat it Does
src/index.tsFull MCP server in TypeScript. Registers 5 tools Bob can call: get_git_diff, run_fuzzer, read_test_logs, an AST static-analysis tool, and apply_patch. Compiles to build/index.js.
tsconfig.jsonTypeScript compiler config. ESM output, Node 18 target.
package.jsonDeclares npm run build (tsc). Depends on @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and zod.

dashboard/ — Command & Control UI

FileWhat it Does
server.jsExpress back-end. Serves the built React SPA, provides SSE endpoints (/events, /events/fuzzer), REST APIs (/api/radar, /api/timeline), handles POST /run-tests to spawn Jest, and uses chokidar to watch the tests/ folder for new files.
client/src/App.jsxRoot React component. Assembles all panels, manages the Run Tests button, wires useSSE + useFuzzerStream hooks together.
client/src/hooks/useSSE.jsTwo custom hooks: useSSE connects to /events and drives shared reducer state; useFuzzerStream opens /events/fuzzer to stream live Jest output into the same reducer.
client/src/components/Individual UI panels: TopBar (header + Run Tests button), StatsRow (KPI counters), LiveLog (scrolling log), MergeConfidence (score widget), MergeRiskRadar (radar chart), AttackSurface (surface status), AgentStatus (A/B agent badges), ThreatTimeline (activity timeline).
client/vite.config.jsVite build config with dev-proxy to the Express API.

.bob/ & .github/ — Config & CI

FileWhat it Does
.bob/prompts/redteam-orchestrator.mdDefines the three agent system prompts (Red Team, Blue Team, Judge) and the orchestration contract. These are injected as LLM system messages by orchestrate.js.
.github/workflows/breakpoint-ci.ymlGitHub Actions workflow. On every PR: builds Docker image → starts container → runs ci-fuzzer.js → posts scorecard → blocks merge on failure.

The Three-Agent Loop

🔴 Red Team
Adversarial Fuzzer
  • Reads route + OpenAPI spec
  • Writes fuzzing & concurrency tests
  • Runs npm test
  • Emits structured ATTACK REPORT JSON
🔵 Blue Team
Security Patch Writer
  • Receives ATTACK REPORT
  • Applies minimal surgical patches
  • Only edits transfer.js
  • Emits PATCH REPORT JSON
⚖️ Judge
Evaluator & Terminator
  • Cross-references both reports
  • Escalates repeat vulns
  • Scores security posture 0–100
  • Emits APPROVED or REJECTED
Round NRed Team generates attacks & runs tests
→
PatchBlue Team closes vulnerabilities
→
VerdictJudge: APPROVED or REJECTED
→
LoopMax 5 rounds; exit 0 on APPROVED, exit 1 if cap hit

What to Run & How

1 · Run the demo-app (target server)

cd breakpoint-ai/demo-app npm install npm start # http://localhost:3000

2 · Run the test suite directly

cd breakpoint-ai/demo-app npm test # jest --detectOpenHandles

3 · Run the full agentic Red/Blue/Judge loop

export WATSONX_API_KEY=your_key export WATSONX_PROJECT_ID=your_project_id # Optional overrides: # export WATSONX_URL=https://us-south.ml.cloud.ibm.com # export MODEL_ID=ibm/granite-3-3-8b-instruct # export MAX_ROUNDS=5 node breakpoint-ai/scripts/orchestrate.js

4 · Run only the CI fuzzer gate (no LLM needed)

cd breakpoint-ai/demo-app && npm install node breakpoint-ai/scripts/ci-fuzzer.js # Set GITHUB_TOKEN + GITHUB_REPOSITORY + PR_NUMBER to post a PR comment

5 · Build & start the MCP server (for Bob integration)

cd breakpoint-ai/mcp-server npm install npm run build # compiles TypeScript → build/index.js node build/index.js # or configure in .bob/mcp.json

6 · Start the live dashboard

# Terminal 1 — API + SSE server cd breakpoint-ai/dashboard && npm install && npm start # port 4242 # Terminal 2 — Vite dev server (hot-reload) cd breakpoint-ai/dashboard/client && npm install && npm run dev # Or serve the pre-built SPA (already built in client/dist): # The Express server automatically serves client/dist at GET *

Key Environment Variables

VariableUsed ByDescription
WATSONX_API_KEYorchestrate.jsIBM Cloud API key — required for the agentic loop
WATSONX_PROJECT_IDorchestrate.jswatsonx.ai project ID — required for the agentic loop
WATSONX_URLorchestrate.jswatsonx.ai endpoint (default: us-south)
MODEL_IDorchestrate.jsGranite model ID (default: ibm/granite-3-3-8b-instruct)
MAX_ROUNDSorchestrate.jsHard cap on loop iterations (default: 5)
DEMO_APP_PATHorchestrate.jsOverride path to demo-app/ directory
GITHUB_TOKENci-fuzzer.jsActions token to post PR comments
GITHUB_REPOSITORYci-fuzzer.js"owner/repo" for GitHub API calls
PR_NUMBERci-fuzzer.jsPull request number for the comment
PORTdemo-app, dashboardServer ports (3000 / 4242 by default)

MCP Server Tools (Bob Integration)

ToolWhat it Exposes to Bob
get_git_diffReturns git diff of demo-app (scoped to one file or full tree, staged or unstaged)
run_fuzzerExecutes the Jest suite inside demo-app/ and returns structured pass/fail summary
read_test_logsParses existing test files; filters by suite (fuzzing/concurrency) and severity
static_analysisRuns regex-based AST rules over source files and returns categorised findings
apply_patchApplies search-replace or full-overwrite patches to demo-app files (with dry-run mode)

Data Flow: Dashboard SSE Events

EventPayloadConsumer Component
log{type, message, ts}LiveLog
score{fuzz, concur, patch}MergeConfidence
status{agent, status}AgentStatus
surface{transfer, validation, race, auth}AttackSurface
radar{axes: [{subject, value}]}MergeRiskRadar
timeline{phase, label, detail, severity}ThreatTimeline
done{exitCode, passed, failed}App (closes stream)

Future Prospects

🎯
Multi-route / multi-service targeting Extend the Red Team to attack any OpenAPI spec, not just the transfer endpoint. Could scan entire microservice meshes.
🧠
Persistent vulnerability memory Store all past ATTACK REPORTs in a vector DB so the Red Team can learn which payloads already worked across projects and skip known-safe paths.
🔌
IDE / VSCode extension Surface the Merge Confidence Scorecard directly inside the editor as a code-lens annotation, powered by the MCP server.
📦
Support for more languages Red Team currently generates Jest/supertest. Could be extended to generate pytest (Python), RSpec (Ruby), or k6 (load testing) suites via pluggable generators.
🔒
SAST + DAST fusion Combine the current dynamic fuzzing with the existing static AST analysis tool to produce a unified CVSS-scored report, linking static findings to dynamic proof-of-exploit test cases.
🔄
Continuous monitoring mode Deploy as a long-running service that re-runs the loop automatically whenever a new commit lands on main, not just on PRs.
📊
Historical security posture trending Persist Judge scores over time, feed them into the dashboard to show a security score trend graph across PRs and releases.
🌐
Multi-tenant SaaS offering The MCP server + dashboard architecture is ready to be multi-tenanted. Add auth, per-project scoping, and a billing layer to offer BreakPoint AI as a security-as-a-service product.
Made with IBM Bob
